data.name: The Bottom of the Well
data.detailed_description:
The Bottom of the Well
A visual novel where Alice steps into a different kind of wonderland.

In The Bottom of the Well, you play as Alice who has just had an unsettingly life-like dream about the end of the world. She retells her experience to her friend in a huge, branching narrative. Although a single play-through might take as little as 20 minutes, experiencing all the possible paths Alice can take through the ruins of her city will take you many hours.

The game is intended to be replayed several times with different permutations of Alice: try playing as a survival-minded lone-wolf, or a social butterfly, or why not attempt the difficult but rewarding romantic route? The stats you select for your Alice in the beginning of the game influences everything from small comments to major choices.

This is an updated, reworked and improved version of my entry to the WAG (Write A Game) Challenge arranged by IGDA's Game Writing SIG, where it placed first in the amateur category. The jury had this to say:

- WINNER: THE BOTTOM OF THE WELL
The Bottom of The Well delivers an entertaining, branched story with interesting options. Alice's dream is genuinely terrifying. The conversations feel natural and appropriate. Players can randomize their character stats, but still negotiate the game with deliberate and meaningful choices. The final game stats give The Bottom of the Well immense replay value. One judge played the game several times to find the "best" ending!

content_descriptors.notes: Contains descriptions of the effects of nuclear war on the human body and society, but all descriptions are flltered through a conversation, and is generally not very explicit. There are no images of gore or violence (some of the images depict ruins, but no bodies or blood).

reviews.review:
The Bottom of the Well is a short visual novel that takes a pretty simple idea and does something surprisingly interesting with it. I play as Alice, a young woman who has just had a disturbing dream about the end of the world, and the whole story is told through her retelling of that dream to a friend. What makes it stand out for me is how much the story changes depending on the choices I make. A single playthrough can be finished in around 20 minutes, but there are a lot of different paths to discover if I keep going back and making different decisions.

The choice system is easily my favourite part. At the beginning I can shape Alice with different statistics, which affects both smaller pieces of dialogue and more important decisions later on. I can make her more focused on survival, more social, or try to pursue the romantic side of the story. I like that these choices are not just there to give me a different sentence every now and then. They can actually change what happens, which makes replaying the story feel worthwhile instead of simply repeating the same thing with a few different lines.

The post apocalyptic setting also works well for such a small game. Alice is exploring the ruins of her city in a dream where the consequences of nuclear war are described through conversations rather than shown through graphic scenes. I think that is a good choice because it lets the writing carry most of the atmosphere. There is something unsettling about hearing people talk about what happened while I slowly realise that this is not really a normal dream. The story has a strange mixture of horror, mystery and almost surreal Alice in Wonderland ideas that gives it more personality than I expected.

The biggest weakness for me is that some of the choices can feel difficult to understand. I can make a decision that seems completely reasonable and still end up with a bad result, which can make certain sections feel like trial and error rather than a choice that I can properly reason through. That is less of a problem once I start learning how the different routes work, but it does mean I sometimes have to replay sections simply because I did not know what the game expected me to do. For a story that is built around meaningful choices, I would have preferred some of the consequences to feel a little more natural.

The short length is another thing I have to take into account. My first playthrough can be over very quickly, so there is not much here if I only intend to experience the story once. The replay value is where most of the content comes from, since I can change Alice's statistics and choices to uncover different routes and endings. There are also 12 Steam achievements, which gives me another reason to explore the different possibilities.

I also appreciate that the game is completely free. That makes the short first playthrough much easier for me to accept because I am not paying for a full length visual novel and then discovering that most of the content depends on replaying it. The writing was also originally developed as an entry for an IGDA game writing challenge before being expanded into this version, which helps explain why the writing and branching structure are such a big part of the experience.

Overall, The Bottom of the Well is a clever little visual novel that I think gets a lot out of its limited scope. I like the unsettling post apocalyptic story, the different ways I can shape Alice, the branching choices and the fact that replaying actually gives me new things to discover. The short individual playthroughs and occasional trial and error keep it from reaching the highest ratings for me, but the free price and strong focus on branching storytelling make up for a lot of that. It is not a huge game, but it has enough ideas packed into it to make me want to see what happens when I make different choices.

Rating: 7/10
